strengths: Novel conceptual contribution: reframes ad-hoc teamwork partner generation as a DCD/UED problem in partner-policy space, generalizing prior approaches (FCP, MEP, E3T) as special cases of a unified framework.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation spanning five Overcooked-AI layouts, a diverse and adversarially constructed evaluation population (BRDiv, planning agents, hardcoded agents, worst-case agents), the harder OGC benchmark, thorough ablations, and a real human-subjects study — this breadth is unusual and strengthens the credibility of the claims.

The proposed variance-based learnability score is simple, requires no extra computation beyond sampling, and is shown empirically to be robust and competitive with more complex alternatives (Gauss-weighted, success-rate-based), providing useful insight for the UED/curriculum-learning community.

The human study is well-designed (double-blind, randomized order, validated survey with high internal consistency, appropriate non-parametric statistical tests with multiple-comparison correction) and shows UPD is preferred both by returns and subjective ratings (adaptiveness, human-likeness, reduced frustration).

Interesting qualitative findings such as emergent convention-breaking/symmetry-breaking behavior that arises organically from the learnability-driven curriculum without explicit design, and clear visualizations of how the curriculum adapts epsilon per layout.
Reasonable reproducibility support: detailed hyperparameter tables, architecture details, compute requirements, and hyperparameter search ranges provided in the appendix.
weaknesses: The human study, while carefully executed, has a small sample (12 participants, 36 games per method across only 3 layouts), which limits generalizability and statistical power despite reaching significance; a larger and/or layout-more-diverse study would strengthen the human-alignment claims.

The paper omits direct comparison against some of the population-based curriculum or open-ended methods cited in the related work (e.g., ROTATE, COLE, RACCOON) that are arguably closer competitors than FCP/MEP/E3T, leaving open whether UPD's gains hold against more recent SOTA baselines.

Baseline training budgets differ (FCP/MEP trained for 2x more environment steps than UPD, with per-layout learning-rate tuning), which, although explained as a fairness measure, complicates a clean comparison and could be read either way regarding UPD's claimed "single hyperparameter set" advantage.

The hand-constructed evaluation population (mixing BRDiv, planning heuristics, hardcoded agents, and random/stay agents) is somewhat ad hoc; its coverage of realistic human-like or truly novel partner behavior is not rigorously justified beyond citing precedent, which affects how representative the reported average returns are of general AHT performance.

On the more challenging OGC benchmark, JUPD's absolute performance still "lags behind" single-layout-trained baselines (as the authors note), suggesting the joint curriculum's benefit is real but limited in the hardest generalization regime.

The method is currently restricted to discrete action spaces and captures only a narrow slice of behavioral diversity (competence and per-action bias via Dirichlet masking); richer partner intentions/goals are left as future work, somewhat narrowing the immediate scope of the contribution.

The reproducibility statement references a code repository but the link/text is missing/truncated ("Our code is available under"), which is a minor but notable oversight for a paper emphasizing reproducibility.

strengths: Extends the well-established unsupervised environment design (UED)/learnability paradigm to the partner space in ad-hoc teamwork, providing a clean population-free alternative to E3T that removes manual tuning of the mixture coefficient epsilon.

Very thorough empirical evaluation: LBF, five Overcooked-AI layouts, and the harder Overcooked Generalisation Challenge (joint partner-environment curriculum), plus a double-blind human-AI user study with proper statistics (Wilcoxon signed-rank, Holm-Bonferroni correction, Cronbach's alpha for internal consistency). The paper reports 282 trained policies in total, indicating substantial experimental effort.

Informative ablations (UPD w/o bias, UPD w/o learnability) and analyses of partner-selection dynamics (Figures 4-6) that provide mechanistic insight, including an interesting emergent 'convention-breaking' phenomenon analogous to hand-engineered methods like Other-Play.

Additional appendix material strengthens the submission: a formal computational-cost comparison against population-based methods, comparison with a recent strong baseline (ROTATE), sensitivity analysis over alternative learnability functions, and a transparency note explaining and correcting earlier bugs.

Human study results are consistent with automated evaluation, showing UPD is rated more adaptive, more human-like, and less frustrating, which strengthens the practical relevance of the claims beyond synthetic partner populations.
weaknesses: The core algorithmic novelty is somewhat incremental: it largely combines an existing partner-generation mechanism (E3T's ego/random mixture) with an existing learnability-based curriculum objective (SFL/Monette et al.'s variance-based scoring), applied to a new axis (partners rather than levels). The conceptual leap, while clean, is a fairly direct transplantation of prior ideas.

The ablation 'UPD w/o learnability' performs nearly as well as full UPD in several Overcooked layouts (e.g., only clearly better in AA), suggesting that much of the benefit comes from large-scale randomized partner generation rather than the learnability mechanism itself, somewhat undercutting the central motivating claim about learnability-driven curricula.

The theoretical justification linking variance-based learnability to expected policy improvement relies on an external, not-yet-published result (Foster et al., 2026) that is asserted rather than derived or empirically validated within this paper.

UPD underperforms population-based/other methods on at least one layout (CRoom) and does not dominate uniformly, and the human study (n=12 participants) is small, which the authors themselves note limits claims of overall superiority.

The partner generator (Alg. 2) still involves hand-specified structural choices (mixture with random policy, Dirichlet-based bias masking, bias probability) — so while explicit mixture-coefficient tuning is removed, the framework is not entirely free of design choices, and its generality to richer/more realistic partner distributions (e.g., human-like biases beyond simple action Dirichlet biases) is untested.

Scalability beyond two-agent settings and beyond relatively simple discrete gridworld domains (LBF, Overcooked, small 5x5 OGC) is not demonstrated, leaving open questions about applicability to larger teams or more complex/continuous domains.
